The fourth: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah. Ibn Juraij and Muqatil said this.

The fifth: Umayyah ibn Khalaf. Ibn Ishaq said this.

The sixth: Ubayy ibn Khalaf. al-Mawardi related this.

The second view: it was revealed in general terms, not concerning a specific individual. Mujahid said this.

The first: they are different. Within this there are seven opinions.

The first: al-humazah is the one who backbites (al-mughtab), and al-lumazah is the one who defames (al-'ayyab). Ibn Abbas said this.

The second: al-humazah is the one who slanders a person to his face, and al-lumazah is the one who defames him when he has turned away. Al-Hasan, 'Ata' and Abu al-'Aliyah said this.

The third: al-humazah is the one who attacks people (al-tta'in fi al-nas), and al-lumazah is the one who attacks people's lineages. Mujahid said this.

The fourth: al-humazah is with the eye, and al-lumazah is with the tongue. Qatadah said this.

The fifth: al-humazah is the one who strikes people with his hand and beats them, and al-lumazah is the one who defames them with his tongue. Ibn Zayd said this.

The sixth: al-humazah is the one who slanders with his tongue, and al-lumazah is the one who defames with his eye. Sufyan al-Thawri said this.

The seventh: al-humazah is the one who backbites, and al-lumazah is the one who attacks a person to his face. Muqatil said this.

The second view: al-humazah is the one who defames and attacks, and al-lumazah is the same. The root of hamz and lamz is pushing (al-daf'). Ibn Qutaybah said this. Likewise al-Zajjaj said: al-humazah al-lumazah is the one who backbites people and disparages them. The poet said:

When I meet you against your will, you grimace at me,
and when I am absent you become the one who slanders and defames.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who gathered wealth and counted it﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Rawh read "jamma'a" with a shadda. The rest read it without the shadda.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and counted it﴾. The majority read the dal with a shadda. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Hasan and Ibn Ya'mur read it without a shadda.

The exegetes have two views on the meaning of the statement.

The first: he counted its number. al-Suddi said this.

The second: he prepared it to suffice him for years. 'Ikrimah said this. al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "addadahu" with a shadda, its meaning is: he counted it for ages. Whoever reads "adadahu" without a shadda, its meaning is: he gathered wealth and numbers, that is, and a people whom he took as helpers.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾. Akhladahu means yukhalliduhu (makes him immortal). The meaning is: he thinks his wealth is preventing him from death, so he acts like one who does not think he will die. "Kalla" (no), that is: his wealth will not make him immortal, nor will it remain for him. ﴿He will surely be thrown﴾, that is, he will surely be cast ﴿into the Huttamah﴾, which is one of the names of Hell. It was so called because it crushes whatever is cast into it, that is, breaks it; it breaks the bone after consuming the flesh. It is said of a glutton: "he is indeed a huttamah." Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman, al-Hasan, Ibn Abi 'Ablah and Ibn Muhaysin read "la-yunbadhanna" with an extended alif, with a kasra on the nun and a shadda, that is: he and his wealth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿which rises over the hearts﴾. That is, it consumes the flesh and skins until it reaches the hearts and burns them. al-Farra' said: its pain reaches the hearts. Ittila' (rising over) and bulugh (reaching) may have one meaning, and the Arabs say: "when did you rise over (talla'ta) our land?" meaning: when did you arrive. Ibn Qutaybah said: "tattali'u 'ala al-af'idah" means: it overcomes and looks over them. He specified the hearts because when pain reaches the heart its owner dies, so He informed that they are in the state of one who dies, yet they do not die. We have already mentioned the explanation of "al-mu'sadah" in Surat al-Balad [90:20].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in extended columns﴾. Hamzah, Khalaf, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, except Hafs, read "'amad" with a damma on the ayn and a sukun on the mim. The exegetes said: these are the pegs of the enclosures that close upon the people of the Fire. "Fi" here means "bi" (with), so the meaning is: closed with columns. Qatadah said: it is so also in the recitation of 'Abd Allah. Muqatil said: the doors were closed upon them, then fastened with iron pegs, so that their distress and heat return upon them. "Mumaddadah" is an adjective of "'amad", meaning: they are extended and lengthened, and they are more firmly fixed than short ones. Qatadah said: they are columns with which they are tormented in the Fire. Abu Salih said: ﴿in extended columns﴾ — he said: the long chains.

Qatadah said: it is so also in the recitation of 'Abd Allah. Muqatil said: the doors were closed upon them, then fastened with iron pegs, so that their distress and heat return upon them. "Mumaddadah" is an adjective of "'amad", meaning: they are extended and lengthened, and they are more firmly fixed than short ones. Qatadah said: they are columns with which they are tormented in the Fire. Abu Salih said: ﴿in extended columns﴾ — he said: the long chains.
